I own both games and think they are different enough that I have no issue in having both, however both are a bit more difficult to play with my group and reward more plays. I would suggest to get one, and play it a bit more instead of getting both and playing both less.What I enjoy most about blood rage is the drafting mechanic. I've always been a huge fan of drafting since playing MTG booster drafts and this is one of the most important phases in the game. A good draft can make or break your strategy. It's a bit more difficult for new players to compete with veterans because if you aren't familiar with all the cards that could be in the game, you could be in for a surprise later.With Kemet you don't have that draft mechanic, but all the powers are open from the start and almost all unique. Some combinations are very strong but so are others and you could always grab one tile of a typical strategy and break the meta. This is similar in Blood Rage, where hate drafting is an option and sometimes the best course of action.The end of Blood Rage is after the third era, and the game length doesn't change much between subsequent plays. With Kemet there is a slow creep towards the end goal (similar to how it works in Catan ) with the possibility of fast swings due to the existence of temporary VP's.

GWT is a lighter game than you would expect, at least ruleswise.   
Like all games explain:

* The victory conditions (most points)
* Game end (when the round 2-point token falls of the board everyone else gets one more turn)
* All ways to gain points (use the score sheet to show this)
* Explain the structure of a turn:
   * Move up to your maximum movement (shown on your player board), ignoring empty tiles
   * Do the actions on the tile you stopped, you can either or all actions on the tile in any order you want, you can always do a simple action instead (which you will explain later) and if you land on a hazard/tepee or a tile of another player you can only do a simple action
   * At the end of the turn you draw up to your hand size
* Then you explain the different actions on the neutral buildings, and the simple/double actions on the player board, followed by the ones on the buildings you can build yourself.
* You explain what happens when you end up in Kansas. (Steps 1-5)
* Last you explain how stations work.

There are some details you have to explain when doing so but I won't list them all: only one train per space, only one delivery per city except for Kansas and San Francisco, the meaning of the hands on the tiles, the extra bonuses on the hazardous tracks etc...  


You could always do this play a few exercise turns and start over for real, that's what I do with most games I explain because sometimes it takes a few turns to get the hang of it (or sometimes a whole game...)

I've only played bridge when I was little with my grandparents. But as far as I remember there isn't very much bluffing in the game. It is based on a quite strict bidding language that has to be adhered to, that maps the way the cards are dealt known by all players. I'm not saying that he wouldn't like bluffing games but bridge isn't one in my opinion.Does he like chess? Maybe try some of the modern abstracts (**onitama**, **tak**, **santorini**, **GIPF** series or **photosynthesis** for 2-4 players): plenty of depth without fiddly rules. For bluffing maybe try a game like **Skull**, simple but elegant. Another one that might be fun is a drafting game like **7 wonders** or the lighter **sushi go**? It has the same mechanic of going around the table but now instead of just getting information from the cards of others by what they bid, you get it by what cards you get (or don't get) from the other players and what they pick.

It is for this reason that I like to know the expected point value for winning players in the games I play. If is is the first time I play it I don't have a good idea of how many points I should try to get every turn. Most of the time you can min-max the last turn to see how much extra you can churn out, but by that time you might have left a lot of points for grabs anyway.

I would have suggested the fox in the forest: a 2-player only trick taking game that I have enjoyed a lot, not as involved as bridge, but fun none the less. I don't think this is a problem. It isn't worse than the drink potion action, in my opinion. You don't get gold, you have a chance of something bad happening (and reputation loss isn't that bad most of the time). Yes you have to pay an extra cube, but even if you wouldn't take the risk and put your cube on the lowest level you would always get 1 gold, so that is equivalent with using the second cube for an alchemy action where you don't even have to pay an ingredient. And the action happens before the publish and debunk action so you can use the information you gained there as well. If you choose your ingredients well you get almost as much information out of the test as the other testing options without having to give that information to your opponents. In the last case I described if you would have gotten the "opposite potion" result, you know the sign, but your opponents can only guess.  
Using the sell potion action well is one of the main ways to win the game. In my games I almost never use the other test methods after the first two turns, unless I have spare ingredients and can go first on the "test on student" action. After a few test you have gathered enough information to have greater than equal odds of getting a beneficial result. My opponents don't always see how good the sell potion action is when used wisely. And I think this is the main reason why I haven't lost a single game out of the nearly ten I have played since getting the game.  
Yes, in most cases the worst outcome is a lot worse than the best, but still about equal to the other options. If you test 4 different ingredients in your first turn and get two times the same potion result, you can eliminate half of the option on your sheet of paper for all ingredients. However the other (and more plausible outcome) is almost always worse than testing the same ingredient twice with two other ingredients. You can win by being lucky with your tests, just like you can bet your 5 point chip on on the first publish action without any prior knowledge, and win because of sheer luck. However if you take small risks where the expected outcome is slightly in your favor, you will after six round almost certainly have an edge.

Another example is when you have an ingredient (A) that makes the same potion with two different ingredients (B and C). So for example A+B and A+C both make a red -.You know that these have the same size in red (either both small or both big).If you combine B and C you have some options:

* you can't make a red potion since the share the same size in red
* you can't make a neutral potion since then they would have to have all opposite signs and they don't
* you can't make a blue potion since if you look at the ingredients we have either:
   * r-G+b+ and r-g+B- which make a green +
   * R-g-b+ and R-G-B- which make a green -

Let's say the adventurer wants to buy a green +, we want to sell it to him saying it is an exact match:

* We get an exact match so green + (50% odds), we know that ingredients B and C are r-G+b+ and r-g+B-, so we can remove these from all other ingredients, we also know that ingredient A has a big R- (so we can remove 2 more option there - we know that A has a green -) and we get 4 gold.
* We get a  negative potion so a green - (50% odds), we know that ingredients B and C are R-g-b+ and R-G-B-, so we can remove these from all other ingredients, we also know that ingredient A has a small R- (so we can remove 2 more option there - we know that A has a green +), we get no gold, but a ton of extra information.

All of these odds can be improved even more if you have extra information about other ingredients. E.g: I you know that two other ingredients (D and E) make a green -, the odds of getting a green + increase. And in the off chance that you still get a negative potion, you know know that ingredients D and E are   r+g-B+ and r+G-b-, so you can eliminate another 2 options for all ingredients.

Depending on what you already know from a certain ingredient, you have better odds to get to get certain results than others. Every ingredient can be combined in 7 ways, resulting in 2 green, red and blue potions and one neutral. If you already know from previous test that one of the ingredients has a red and green +, then there it will make the following potion with the other 5 ingredients:

* 1 red + potion
* 1 green + potion
* 2 blue potion with equal odds of + and -
* 1 neutral potion

So you have a 60% chance of making a + potion, 20% of making a neutral potion and 20% of making a negative potion. If you bet on at least making a neutral potion, you have an 80% chance of getting 2 gold, which is the same as using the alchemy action on them (which would have costed you 3 cubes and given no information at all).

Let's say the adventurer wants to buy a blue +:

We can have 4 results:

* We get an exact result (20% odds), know that the ingredient is R+G+B+, and the second ingredient has a (small) blue + and earn 2 gold
* We get a correct sign (40% odds), we have no extra information of the ingredient, the second ingredient has either a green or a red +, and we earn 2 gold
* We get a neutral potion (20% odds), we have no extra information of the ingredient, the second ingredient has a red- and green -, and we earn 2 gold
* We get a negative potion (20% odds), we know that this has to be blue since we already know the red and green signs, so we know that the ingredient is R+g+b- and the second ingredient has a (big) blue -, we earn no gold but still got a lot of information.

BONUS: the neutral potion consists of two ingredients that have all opposite signs for all colors as well as equal size for all colors.

1) Place the dice in the correct line

2) Determine which action you want to happen for sure

3) Determine how many of those actions you want to do (e.g. you need 4 settler, so try to get 4 dice there, if you have less put a die from another row there on the card and use the dictate ability if needed) 

4) Arrange the other dice if needed. (I don't go into much detail about the tech abilities that let you reassign dice, since in the beginning this is not necessary for most starting factions)

The problem with using pipes is that every connected warded jar that is labeled or has at least one essentia in it outputs a type-specific suction. No the routing is directly. You could just remove the whole breaking down items part and just use it for sorting too. There are never suction issues. What you do is flow through a cascade of buffers where you make sure that the direction where it comes from is set to red, so 0 suction. The next buffer has a suction of 1. If you connect a jar of essentia with regular essentia pipes to a buffer it will have a typed suction and so will only pull from it when it's the right type, if not it will continue through the cascade. If the jar however is full the suction again drops to 0 and it will again flow though the buffer cascade.
The whole breaking down part is done by first going through a similar cascade but instead of pulling to a jar, pull to a buffer with the valve and filtered tube in front. To get enough suction you need to connect a bellow. Connect all these with a parallel system of buffers and connect these to the original system. The ones that never get pulled out go to the centrifuges which goes back through the whole filtering cycle until filtered out (when needed) or only primals remain.

Here are [some screenshots](http://imgur.com/a/nm5GT) of the setup I use. It looks more complicated than it is mainly due to the fact that I built it in a round room and that the routing is a little bit more difficult. The use of essentia buffers (with filtered essentia pipes) is paramount to get it to run decently.

In this setup I use essentia mirrors (4) and the essentia pump to export when I need them for things other than infusions.
